# Cost burden and instability {#sec-burden}

<!-- Purpose: cost burden trends and housing instability — burden by tenure/race-ethnicity/
     income (ACS + CHAS + PUMS), wage affordability (OEWS), evictions, delinquency, and PIT
     homelessness counts. Theme-based takeaway H2s; static ggplot only; "Since 2022" callout
     per section; fig-alt throughout. Built in Task 11. -->



## Renter cost burden is climbing again since 2019


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Renter cost burden is climbing again since 2019](burden_files/figure-html/fig-burden-trend-1.png){#fig-burden-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Two stacked bar charts of cost burden shares for renters and owners in the Richmond region across the 2010-2014, 2015-2019, and 2020-2024 ACS periods, with 2010-2014 shown muted. Renter bars dip from 51.2 percent burdened in 2010-2014 to 49.9 percent in 2015-2019, then rise to 51.3 percent in 2020-2024. Owner bars show the burdened share falling from 26 percent to 20 percent over the same span, with no rebound.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Renter cost burden eased to 50% by 2015–19 but has since climbed back to 51% in 2020–24 — a 1% increase in just five years.**
- Severe burden drives the recent rise: severely cost-burdened renters grew from 24.5 percent of all renters in 2015–19 to 26% in 2020–24.
- Owners kept moving the opposite direction: the burdened owner share fell from 21% in 2015–19 to 20% in 2020–24, continuing a decade-long decline from 26 percent in 2010–14.
- Because the renter population grew while the burdened share rose, the count of cost-burdened renter households climbed from 66,647 in 2015–19 to 73,767 in 2020–24 — a faster five-year rise than the change across the full prior decade.

::: {.callout-important}
## Since 2022
The 2022 Framework reported cost-burdened renters up by almost 1,900 households and cost-burdened owners down by more than 7,200 since 2015 (Fig 10.1). This update finds the same split, larger on the renter side: burdened renter households up 10,349 (+16.3%) and burdened owner households down 7,742 (-11.4%) from 2010–2014 to 2020–2024. **Caveat:** the 2022 figures rode on the 2016–2020 ACS with a 2015 base year; this update compares non-overlapping 2010–2014 and 2020–2024 windows, so the magnitudes are directionally comparable but not measured on the same yardstick.
:::

## Renter cost burden tops 50 percent in Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield alike


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Renter cost burden tops 50 percent in Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield alike](burden_files/figure-html/fig-burden-locality-1.png){#fig-burden-locality fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dodged bar chart of 2020-2024 renter cost burden shares for Virginia and the four primary localities. Each geography shows two bars: cost-burdened (30-49 percent of income) and severely cost-burdened (50 percent or more). Shares cluster between 22 and 28 percent for both categories everywhere; Richmond has the highest severe share at 28 percent, and Hanover is lowest overall.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Total renter cost burden is nearly uniform across the three largest localities: 52 percent in Chesterfield, 52 percent in Richmond, and 52 percent in Henrico — this is a regional condition, not a city problem.**
- Richmond has the largest severe tilt: 28 percent of city renters pay half or more of their income toward housing, against 24 percent in Henrico and 25 percent in Chesterfield.
- Hanover is the outlier at 45 percent total renter burden, still well above the owner rate anywhere in the region.
- The three largest localities all exceed the statewide renter burden rate of 49 percent; Hanover sits below it.
- Estimates for Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan are suppressed: every renter burden cell in those localities carries a CV above 30 (Low reliability). Their small renter counts (roughly 300–1,300 renter households each) cannot support reliable shares at this cut; HUD's CHAS tables cover them at coarser income-band cuts, in the AMI-band figure below.

## Cost burden is nearly universal below 30 percent of area median income


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cost burden is nearly universal below 30 percent of area median income](burden_files/figure-html/fig-chas-ami-1.png){#fig-chas-ami fig-align='left' fig-alt='Faceted bar chart of cost burden shares by household income band, as a percent of area median income (AMI), for owner and renter households in the 8-locality Richmond region. At 0-30% AMI, 86 percent of renters and 79 percent of owners are cost-burdened, most of them severely. Burden falls steadily at each higher income band, dropping to about half of renters and a third of owners at 50-80% AMI, and to under 4 percent of either group above 100% AMI.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **NA of renters and NA of owners below 30 percent of area median income are cost-burdened, and most of them severely: NA of renters and NA of owners in this band pay half or more of income toward housing.**
- Burden falls sharply as income rises: by 50-80% AMI, NA of renters and NA of owners are burdened; above 100% AMI, fewer than NA of renters and NA of owners are.
- Renters are more burdened than owners at every income band below 100% AMI, widest at the bottom of the scale.
- These are regional totals pooled across all 8 Richmond region localities, so every income band here is measured at a reliable scale — including for Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan, whose renter counts are too small for the locality-level ACS cut above.

## Severe burden is rising in the counties, easing in Richmond


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Severe burden is rising in the counties, easing in Richmond](burden_files/figure-html/fig-severe-trend-1.png){#fig-severe-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of the severely cost-burdened renter share for the four primary localities across the 2010-2014, 2015-2019, and 2020-2024 ACS periods, with the earliest period muted. All four localities dip in 2015-2019, then diverge: Chesterfield rises from 21 to 25 percent between 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, Hanover from 19 to 22 percent, and Henrico from 22 to 24 percent. Richmond instead declines from 30 to 28 percent over the same recent span, though it remains highest overall.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Severe renter burden jumped in every primary locality except Richmond between 2015–19 and 2020–24: Chesterfield rose 4.2 points to 25 percent, Hanover rose 2.7 points to 22 percent, and Henrico rose 1.9 points to 24 percent.**
- Richmond moved the other way, easing from 30 percent in 2015–19 to 28 percent in 2020–24 — even as it still carries the region's largest severe-burden caseload, about 15,800 renter households.
- All four localities had dipped in 2015–19 before this recent runup, so the full-decade change looks smaller than the last five years alone.
- Chesterfield added the most severely burdened renter households of any locality since 2015–19 — up about 1,600 (from 5,962 to 7,599), a 27 percent increase in five years.
